cards.title: A sharp knife is a safe knife
cards.body: A dull blade slips, and slips cause cuts. A sharp knife goes exactly where you push it, so you stay in control. If your knife crushes a tomato instead of slicing it, it is time to sharpen.

cards.title: The claw grip saves fingertips
cards.body: Curl your fingertips under like a claw and rest your knuckles against the flat side of the blade. The knife rides along your knuckles, and your fingertips stay tucked safely behind them. It feels weird for a week, then it is automatic.
Put a damp paper towel under your cutting board. A board that slides is an accident waiting to happen — the towel locks it in place for free.

Dicing an onion, the safe way: cut it in half through the root, peel, and lay each half flat-side down. Make horizontal cuts, then vertical cuts, keeping the root end intact as a handle. Finally slice across. The claw grip guides every cut.

cards.q: Why is a sharp knife safer than a dull one?
choices: It cuts exactly where you push it instead of slipping
cards.explain: A sharp edge bites into food and tracks straight. A dull edge skates across the surface — and your hand is usually in the way.

flashcards.back: Curling your fingertips under and guiding the knife along your knuckles, so the blade never meets your fingertips.

flashcards.front: How do you stop a cutting board sliding?
flashcards.back: Put a damp paper towel or cloth underneath it.
Honing straightens the blade's edge (do it often); sharpening grinds a new edge (do it rarely).

flashcards.front: Which knife does most kitchen work?
flashcards.back: The chef's knife — 8 inches of all-rounder for chopping, slicing, and dicing.

questions.q: Your tomato squishes instead of slicing. What is wrong?
questions.explain: A sharp knife slices cleanly. Crushing means the edge is dull — sharpen it, don't press harder.

questions.q: Where do your fingertips go in the claw grip?
choices: Spread flat on top of the food
Curled under, knuckles against the blade
questions.explain: Fingertips tuck under like a claw; the flat of the blade rides your knuckles. Nothing sharp ever touches a fingertip.

questions.q: The board keeps sliding on the counter. Fix it?
choices: Hold it with your other hand
questions.explain: A damp towel grips both surfaces and locks the board down. Holding it puts your hand next to the blade.

questions.q: How often should you hone a knife you use daily?
choices: Every time you cook, a few strokes
questions.explain: A few honing strokes before each session keep the edge straight. Sharpening (grinding) is the rare, heavy job.

questions.q: You are carrying a knife across the kitchen. Safe way?
choices: Toss it in the sink when done
Blade down, at your side, saying 'behind'
Blade up so people see it
questions.explain: Blade points down at your side, and you call out so nobody steps into you. A knife in a sink full of water is a hidden trap.

cards.title: Heat is a dial, not a switch
cards.body: High heat sears and browns; medium heat cooks through; low heat simmers gently. Most home mistakes come from the dial being too high — smoking oil and burnt outsides with raw insides.

cards.title: Salt in layers, not at the end
cards.body: Salt each component as you cook it: the pasta water, the vegetables, the protein. Food salted at every stage tastes seasoned all the way through; food salted once at the end tastes salty on the outside and bland inside.
Taste as you go. Your tongue is the only timer that never lies — a quick taste after each addition tells you exactly what the dish still needs.

Searing chicken thighs: pat them dry (moisture is the enemy of browning), heat the pan until the oil shimmers, lay thighs skin-side down, and do not touch them for 6 minutes. The crust forms while you wait. Flip once, finish in the oven.

cards.q: When should minced garlic go into a hot pan?
choices: In the last 30-60 seconds of cooking
Only after the dish is plated
cards.explain: Garlic burns in under a minute over high heat and turns bitter. Add it late, when the pan has cooled slightly or other ingredients cushion it.

flashcards.back: Browning the surface of meat over high heat for flavor and crust — it does not 'seal in juices.'
Food keeps cooking from residual heat after leaving the pan — pull meat a few degrees before target.
'Everything in its place' — prepping and measuring all ingredients before the heat goes on.

flashcards.front: Why pat meat dry before searing?
flashcards.back: Surface moisture steams instead of browning. Dry surface = real crust.

questions.q: Your chicken is burnt outside and raw inside. What happened?
questions.explain: Blasting heat chars the outside before the inside cooks through. Medium heat gives the center time to catch up.

questions.q: Why salt the pasta water instead of just the sauce?
choices: The pasta itself absorbs seasoning as it cooks
questions.explain: Pasta cooked in bland water stays bland inside no matter how good the sauce is. Salty water seasons every bite.

questions.q: The pan is smoking before the food goes in. What now?
choices: Pull it off the heat and let it cool down
questions.explain: Smoking oil is past its limit and will taste bitter. Cool the pan, wipe it, and start over at a lower setting.

questions.q: You added garlic first and now it tastes bitter. Why?
choices: Garlic burns in under a minute over high heat
questions.explain: Minced garlic goes from golden to burnt fast. It belongs in the pan late, not first.

questions.q: The dish tastes flat but not under-salted. What is missing?
choices: Acid — a squeeze of lemon or splash of vinegar
questions.explain: When salt alone does not fix it, acid is usually the answer. A little brightness wakes up every other flavor.

cards.title: Start from the plate, not the recipe
cards.body: A complete plate needs three things: a protein (chicken, beans, eggs), a vegetable, and a starch (rice, potatoes, bread). Pick one from each column and you already have dinner — the recipe just fills in details.

cards.title: Work backwards from serving time
cards.body: Decide when you eat, then schedule everything in reverse. Rice takes 20 minutes, chicken 25, salad 5 — so rice goes on first, chicken next, salad last. The meal lands hot all at once instead of in sad, cold waves.
Rest meat 5-10 minutes after cooking. Juices that were driven to the center settle back through the meat. Cut too early and they flood the board instead of staying in your dinner.

A 25-minute chicken dinner: 0:00 — oven on, rice in the pot. 0:05 — chicken thighs in the oven. 0:20 — chop a quick salad while everything finishes. 0:25 — rest the chicken 5 minutes, plate it all together. One timeline, zero panic.

cards.q: Why let meat rest after cooking?
choices: Juices redistribute instead of spilling out
It cools to a safe temperature
cards.explain: Heat drives juices to the center. Resting lets them settle back through the meat — slice early and they pour onto the board.

flashcards.front: What three things make a complete plate?
flashcards.back: A protein, a vegetable, and a starch.
So the juices redistribute through the meat instead of flooding the cutting board.

flashcards.front: How do you time a multi-part meal?
flashcards.back: Work backwards from serving time, starting the longest-cooking item first.

flashcards.front: Salt, acid, fat, heat — what are these?
flashcards.back: The four levers for balancing flavor. If a dish is dull, one of them is missing.

questions.q: You have chicken, broccoli, and rice. What is missing for a complete plate?
questions.explain: Chicken is the protein, broccoli the vegetable, rice the starch. That is a full plate already.

questions.q: Rice takes 20 min, fish takes 10, salad takes 5. Dinner at 7:00. When does the rice start?
questions.explain: Longest item first: rice at 6:40, fish at 6:50, salad at 6:55 — everything lands at 7:00.

questions.q: You slice the steak immediately and juice floods the board. Lesson?
questions.explain: The juices needed time to settle back in. Patience keeps them in the meat where they belong.

questions.q: The soup tastes rich but dull. Salt did not fix it. Next move?
choices: Add acid — lemon juice or vinegar
questions.explain: Salt, acid, fat, heat: when a rich dish tastes flat, brightness from acid is almost always the missing lever.

questions.q: Why chop everything before turning on the heat?
choices: Once cooking starts there is no time to prep
questions.explain: That is mise en place. Stir-fry waits for no one — if you are still chopping, the garlic is already burning.
